name: Mere-exposure effect
statement: Seeing something repeatedly makes people like it more, with no need for the repetitions to have taught them anything about it.
meaning: The word mere is carrying the claim. Liking something more after learning it is useful is unremarkable; the proposal is that bare repeated exposure, with no reward and no new information, is enough on its own. Zajonc's demonstrations used nonsense words, Chinese-like characters and unfamiliar faces precisely so that nothing could be learned from a second look. The effect has been reported for stimuli presented too briefly to be consciously recognised, which if it holds means the preference forms without the person knowing what they are preferring.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The monograph is "Attitudinal effects of mere exposure". Zajonc also pointed at correlational evidence outside the laboratory, including the relationship between how often a word appears in a language and how positive its meaning is.

evidence: The standard procedure shows a set of unfamiliar items varying numbers of times, then asks how much the participant likes each one. Liking rises with the number of prior showings. The paradigm is easy to run, has been run for over fifty years, and appears across pictures, words, sounds and faces, which is why the meta-analytic question is not whether the effect exists but what shape it has.

replication.headline: A meta-analysis of 268 curve estimates found the effect is real and that it is an inverted U, so more exposure stops helping and starts hurting.
replication.detail: Montoya and colleagues pooled 268 curve estimates from 81 articles and modelled liking as a function of number of exposures rather than as a single difference. The relationship came out inverted-U shaped: liking rises with repetition, peaks, and then declines. That pattern held for visual stimuli but not auditory ones, for exposure durations under ten seconds or over one minute, for both homogeneous and heterogeneous presentation, and when ratings were collected after all stimuli had been shown. So the verdict is mixed in a specific sense. The effect is not in doubt; the simple monotonic version of it, which is the version that gets cited, is.

study.cite: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., & Lauber, E. A. (2017). A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking. Psychological Bulletin, 143(5), 459-498.

limits: No pooled effect size is printed here because the meta-analysis models a curve rather than estimating a single difference, and quoting one number for an inverted U would misdescribe its main finding. The 268 figure counts curve estimates and the 81 counts articles. The moderator results also mean the effect should not be assumed to transfer between modalities: the shape held for what people see and not for what they hear, which matters for anyone reasoning from this literature about repeated advertising or repeated music. And a meta-analysis inherits whatever publication bias sits in its inputs, which for a fifty-year-old effect with an easy paradigm is a real concern.
misreadings: The effect is routinely cited as though more exposure always means more liking, which the meta-analysis specifically contradicts. It also gets used to explain advertising wearout and its opposite at the same time, which should be a warning: a claim that predicts both outcomes predicts neither. And the subliminal version, where preferences form for stimuli shown too briefly to recognise, is the most-quoted and least-secure part of the literature; it rests on a smaller body of work than the ordinary version does.

sources.text: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt.2), 1-27.
